extraction_text: Nakula swiftly annihilated the army in battle, and Shakuni, son of Subala, angrily charged forward, shouting 'Stop! Stop!'
Shakuni and Nakula, both eager to kill each other, drew their bows and shot sharp arrows at one another.
Shakuni rapidly fired a shower of arrows, and Nakula displayed his skilled martial arts in the fierce battle.
The two warriors became covered with arrow wounds, resembling two thorny silk-cotton trees, glaring at each other with blood-red eyes.
Shakuni, enraged, shot a sharp barbed arrow that struck Nakula in the chest.
Nakula, heavily wounded by Shakuni, collapsed on his chariot seat and fainted.
Seeing his formidable enemy in this desperate state, Shakuni roared like thunder from a summer cloud.
Nakula regained consciousness and charged at Shakuni again like the wide-open jaws of Death.
Nakula, filled with rage, shot sixty arrows at Shakuni, then one hundred iron arrows at his chest.
Nakula shot and broke the grip of Shakuni's bow, then quickly shot down the banner from his chariot.
Shakuni, severely wounded, collapsed on his chariot seat. His charioteer saw him unconscious and quickly drove him away from the front lines.
The sons of Pritha and their followers cheered. Nakula, having defeated his enemy, angrily told his charioteer to take him to Drona's army.
Shikhandin attempted to approach Drona, and Kripa, son of Sharadvat, immediately rushed forward vigorously.
Seeing Kripa reach Drona's side, Shikhandin shot nine crescent-headed arrows at this enemy-subduer.
To please your sons, the teacher first shot five arrows at him, then twenty more.
A terrible battle erupted between the two, like the battle between Shambara and Indra during the war between gods and demons.
The two great warriors covered the sky with nets of arrows, making the terrifying night even more frightening.
Shikhandin shot a half-moon arrow that broke Kripa's great bow along with its string and the arrow on it.
Kripa, enraged, threw a terrifying golden-shafted spear with a sharp, polished point.
Shikhandin released many sharp arrows that broke the flying spear, causing the radiant spear to fall to the ground.
Gautama (Kripa) raised another bow and covered Shikhandin with sharp arrows.
Shikhandin, covered by Kripa's arrows, collapsed onto his chariot seat.
Kripa, son of Sharadvata, fired many arrows in succession, eager to kill Shikhandin.
Panchalas and Somakas surrounded Shikhandin as he withdrew from battle.
Duryodhana's sons led a large army to surround Kripa.
A fierce night battle resumed with chariots, cavalry, elephants, and infantry clashing.

extraction_text: In the confusion of night battle, fathers killed sons, sons killed fathers, uncles killed nephews, and friends killed friends.

relationships: Familial and friendly relationships broken by battle

relationships: Dhrishtadyumna (commander of Pandava army) vs Drona (Kaurava commander)

extraction_text: Duryodhana's sons fought from all directions to rescue the surrounded Drona.
Two massive armies clashed in the night like two stormy oceans meeting.

relationships: Final major confrontation in Drona Parva

extraction_text: Prince of Panchala (Matsya Kingdom) fired five arrows at Drona's chest and roared like a lion.
Drona retaliated with twenty-five arrows and cut off Matsya's bow with a crescent-headed arrow.
Matsya, enraged, took another superior bow intending to kill Drona.
Matsya shot a terrifying arrow at Drona, which was intercepted and shattered into twelve pieces by Karna.
Karna, Ashvatthaman, Drona, Shalya, Dushasana, Duryodhana, and Shakuni collectively attacked Matsya with arrows.
Matsya counterattacked all seven warriors, shooting three arrows at each, and additional arrows at Drona, Ashvatthaman, Karna, and Duryodhana.
The seven warriors retaliated by shooting five arrows each at Matsya.
Vrishasena shot arrows at Matsya, shouting 'Stand! Stand!', and Matsya retaliated by shooting three sharp golden-feathered arrows at him.
Matsya beheaded Vrishasena with a crescent-headed arrow.
Matsya broke Karna's bow with a crescent-headed arrow, enraging Karna who then attacked Matsya with a stream of arrows.
Six warriors (Karna, Ashvatthaman, Drona, Shalya, Dushasana, Duryodhana) surrounded Matsya, intending to kill him.
Satyaki of the Dasharha tribe approached Matsya while showering arrows.
Satyaki charged forward, and Karna shot ten straight-flying arrows at him.
Satyaki shot ten arrows back at Karna and challenged him to stand and fight.
Satyaki and Karna engaged in a terrible battle, compared to the battle between Bali and Indra.
Karna's son Vrishasena, fully armed with Duryodhana's army, surrounded Satyaki and shot sharp arrows from all directions.
Satyaki, enraged, blocked their weapons and Karna's arrows, hitting Vrishasena in the chest.
Vrishasena, deeply wounded by the arrow, dropped his bow and fainted in his chariot.
Karna, thinking Vrishasena was dead, grieved his son's loss and fiercely attacked Satyaki.
Satyaki, struck by Karna, immediately shot many sharp arrows at Karna in succession.
Satyaki shot ten arrows at Karna and seven at Vrishasena, breaking their leather guards and bows.

attributes.action: Simultaneous attack on father and son

extraction_text: Karna and Vrishasena restrung new bows and shot sharp arrows at Satyaki from all directions.
The earth-shaking sound of Arjuna's Gandiva bow was heard during the battle.
Karna told Duryodhana that Arjuna had killed all the Shibi and Pulastya warriors and was making Gandiva roar again.
Karna described Arjuna's chariot rumbling like Indra's chariot and Arjuna performing heroic deeds.
Karna reported that the Bharata army was completely scattered and couldn't be reassembled.
Karna warned that their army, when encountering Arjuna, would be like a broken ship in the ocean.
Karna described hundreds of warrior chiefs being hit by Gandiva's arrows, fleeing and shouting like thunder in the midnight sky.
Karna reported cries of 'Alas! Alas!', lion roars, and various shouts surrounding Arjuna's chariot.
Karna proposes a strategy to defeat the enemy by capturing or killing key warriors Satyaki and Shikhandin.
Duryodhana, following Karna's advice, orders Shakuni to advance against Arjuna with a large force including elephants, chariots, and infantry.
Duryodhana commands Shakuni to kill the Pandavas, expressing his hope for victory rests on him.
Shakuni advances with Duryodhana's sons and the army towards the Pandavas, leading to renewed battle.
Karna leads a large army and quickly attacks Satyaki, showering him with arrows, while the Pandava army surrounds Satyaki for protection.
Drona engages in a large-scale night battle with the valiant Shikhandin and the Panchalas.
Furious warriors swiftly advance on Satyaki's chariot, surrounding him with chariots, cavalry, and elephants, and shower him with arrows while roaring to intimidate him.
Satyaki (Sātyaki) fought fiercely against the rapidly advancing enemies, shooting many sharp arrows.
Satyaki shot down many heads with straight arrows and severed elephant trunks, horse necks, and weapon-holding arms with horse-hoof arrows.
Duryodhana heard the terrifying screams and ordered his charioteer to drive toward the source of the sound where Satyaki was.

extraction_text: After routing this army, Dhrishtadyumna shone brilliantly like Indra among the gods.
